strengths: Using label propagation and label spreading within density-ratio Bayesian optimization is a coherent, potentially useful combination. The paper explains its relationship to BORE, LFBO, and established semi-supervised methods, and accommodates both sampled unlabeled points and fixed candidate pools.

The empirical results are promising: Figures 2–3 show substantial improvements on several synthetic problems, and Figure 6 shows faster progress on NATS-Bench. Comparisons include multiple BORE/LFBO classifiers and GP acquisitions, with 20 repetitions and standard errors.

The appendices provide useful sensitivity studies covering bandwidth, unlabeled sample counts, sampling distributions, and pool subsampling. Including a no-unlabeled-data comparison and acknowledging computational limitations are valuable.
weaknesses: The central claim that semi-supervised learning remedies inadequate exploration is not convincingly established. Section 3.1 defines overconfidence through the concentration of high class probabilities, but neither decision-region coverage nor escape from local optima is measured systematically. Enlarging a high-probability region does not itself establish better exploration under an argmax acquisition rule. The illustrative trajectories and regret improvements support empirical usefulness more strongly than the proposed explanation.

The cluster-assumption justification is unsound as stated. Sampling truncated Gaussians around evaluated points does not ensure that high-density connected regions share the changing objective-threshold label; nearby centers can have opposite labels. Uniformly sampled synthetic pools likewise provide no density valleys aligned with those labels. Appendix C acknowledges that the cited i.i.d. learning bounds do not apply to sequential BO, and supplies no replacement argument establishing decision-region expansion or improved optimization.

The experiments do not adequately isolate the contribution of unlabeled data from the choice of kernel classifier and bandwidth adaptation. Figure 11 sometimes favors the no-transduction variant, especially on Bukin6, but fixes beta at 0.5 while the main experiments learn it. A suitably tuned supervised kernel baseline and matched bandwidth and query-selection ablations are needed on the main benchmarks. This matters particularly because the contribution is chiefly the combination of existing components.

Some evaluation settings limit the broader conclusions. Continuous sampling is evaluated only on four two-dimensional functions, and tabular improvements are less consistent. The MNIST representation is trained on 440,000 images to predict the exact three-digit objective label. Although training and test splits are separate, this supplies substantial objective-specific supervision; a baseline ranking candidates directly with that pretrained classifier is needed to interpret the optimization benefit.

Reproduction is impeded by missing consequential details: input scaling and categorical encoding, bandwidth optimization bounds and initialization, propagation tolerance and iteration limits, the label-spreading clamping factor, and adaptation of the stated L-BFGS-B procedure to finite pools. There is also a correctable mathematical inconsistency: the entrywise definition of P implies WD^{-1}, whereas the text states D^{-1}W before using P transposed in Equation 7.

The practical computational trade-off remains unclear. Dense graph propagation, repeated bandwidth optimization, and 1,000 acquisition restarts can introduce substantial overhead. Figure 13 compares internal subsampling settings with fixed bandwidth, rather than end-to-end runtime against the baselines under the main experimental configuration. Together with the unresolved attribution and justification issues, this makes weak rejection more appropriate despite the promising performance curves.
